channel.title: Comments on: Mathematics has changed. Let’s act like it
channel.description: Updates on my research and expository papers, discussion of open problems, and other maths-related topics. By Terence Tao

item.title: By: Anonymous
item.dc:creator: Anonymous
item.content:encoded:
In reply to Gordon Royle.

In person math competitions. Just like there are for high school and undergraduate students, there can be for junior researchers.

With enough universities on board, there could be a system of competitions for a range of difficulty levels, and topics. Graduate students, and post, can take part on them, just like comprehensive exams, but every year. The rankings provide credit on the topic of the competition. Exam A can be issued by university U, but administered at multiple universities and institutions simultaneously. So, that takes case of the volume.

No evaluation system is perfect, but in person exams have the desired property of being in person.

item.title: By: Anonymous
item.dc:creator: Anonymous
item.content:encoded:
Note there is also a difference between knowing mathematics deeply and explaining it fluently; they are related but different skills. Ideally I want both, but it is the first that I ultimately value more highly.

This is an important point. It is easy to do interviews, at least at the last stages of hiring, but what those interviews target can be very subtle. If it becomes just “talk about this”, those characters who are “good at talking” have an advantage. That’s OK, in part. People good at teaching pass through that sieve. Now, one doesn’t want the hiring process to be permeable to the “good at talking, but not good at doing (unassisted)”.

So, I would add a little more precision to the “knowing mathematics” and clarify that problem solving skills go in there, not only an enumeration of results, and ideas.

item.title: By: Anonymous
item.dc:creator: Anonymous
item.content:encoded:
Here’s a thought experiment: suppose major AI firms did not exist yet. Suppose the mathematical community had seen the potential uses of the technology, and sought to develop this as shared infrastructure. We’d recognize the potential for the good, bad and disruptive [it doesn’t take a savant or a pessimist to predict the disruption].
How would we have approached this? How would we decide to manage the transition? What norms would we change?

We’re presently in fully reactive mode, rushing on someone else’s timeline. This is because we’ve taken as axiomatic that (a) AI adoption is necessary and (b) commercial AI lab practices should dictate the pace and nature of adoption.

What would a more intentional, thoughtful adoption of the technology look like?

I’ll give a small example of an intentional change we might have considered. We’d have discussed it, piloted it, and then decided to adopt or not.

At present, most conferences in my field don’t have many 50-60 minute talks. The bulk are in the 20-25 minute range. The short talks may be inadequate for communicating one’s deep understanding about results of ever-increasing sophistication [AI is supposed to help with the latter]. Deep questioning doesn’t happen either.

Well, maybe we should change the format of conferences. Maybe have a vast number of parallel sessions, with each talk being sufficiently long so as to reveal understanding and allow meaningful discussion? Maybe plenary speakers give 15 minute talks [we agree they know of what they speak], and everyone else gives hour-long talks?

Andrew Ng has a very interesting proposal around how we may revise dissemination: https://proofsandprompts.com/2026/11/01/a-new-system-of-accreditation/

All of this to say: I’d be much more optimistic about the miracles of AI, if I were convinced that we’re not just in purely reactive mode, our decision-making tied to the vagaries of IPOs.

-Nilima Nigam

item.title: By: nobody
item.dc:creator: nobody
item.content:encoded: I am increasingly dissatisfied with how narrowly we discuss AI and mathematics. Mathematics is an early warning of upheaval across society, and keeping this debate inside mathematics misses the point. Even planning solely for mathematicians must start with how AI will transform the society they depend on. We have repeatedly underestimated AI. Stop waiting until the disruption becomes undeniable, when society may already have lost its chance to prepare. The world changes before evidence catches up—even frontier labs must take time to discover what their models can do, and outsiders learn still later. My position: err on the side of overestimating AI and prepare now for rapid disruption across society.

item.title: By: Anonymous
item.dc:creator: Anonymous
item.content:encoded:
In reply to Gordon Royle.

while I agree with you that the human touch is lost, I do not think it is reasonably possible to give fair consideration to everybody who would want a tenure position at even a middling university in a middling country. There are SO MANY people in this world, you simply cannot consider all the many talented individuals that will apply.

I think the only fair way to deal with this fact is to select the 5 person shortlist entirely at random, given some low base criteria filter. Trying to filter people at all is going to be by definition dehumanizing and likely to filter out the very rare jewels you are looking for in the first place – if they were both brilliantly talented and had a stellar CV they wouldn’t be applying to you but to some other place instead

item.title: By: David Roberts
item.dc:creator: David Roberts
item.content:encoded:
Evaluate all work as if it is AI-assisted.

But what if someone chooses not to use AI for their research? How will they be assessed compared to someone who happily accelerates/assists their progress with the tools? How does one equitably recognise the work and ideas and promise of such an “AI vegan” if you insist on assuming that their relative-to-AI slower progress was somehow their poor use/application of it?

I have no answers, but surely this type of insistence is the kind of driver that penalises people who otherwise would have been considereed perfectly solid citizens, even if not the rising stars of their field, who don’t want to use AI?
